title: Dukaan v0.1 — the stock list
brief: Amina runs a small shop. She keeps stock in her head and on paper slips. She wants a program that shows her stock list on screen: item names and prices, clear enough to read at a glance. Build version 0.1 — it only displays the list. This is the first brick of the system you will grow for the whole course.
deliverables: A dukaan.py file that runs with python dukaan.py and shows the stock list.
The program's output, copied into your notes or a screenshot.
A two-line README: what the program does and how to run it.
acceptance: python dukaan.py runs with no errors.
The shop name appears on the first line.
Three items appear, each with the correct price.
Changing a price changes only that line in the output.
You can explain every line to another person without reading.

title: A reliable unit conversion desk
brief: A shop employee needs a small converter for distances and temperatures. Build a program with a clearly selected conversion, labelled inputs and outputs, and helpful handling of invalid input. Keep distance validation separate from temperature rules: negative Celsius values are valid, while the project's distance contract rejects negative distances.
deliverables: A converter supporting kilometres to metres and Celsius to Fahrenheit.
A written input contract for both conversions.
A test-results table with valid, zero, negative, and non-numeric examples.
A short explanation of types and unit names in the implementation.
acceptance: Both conversion formulas produce the documented reference results.
Outputs include the input and output units.
Invalid numeric text produces a useful error message.
Negative temperature and distance inputs follow their separate contracts.
A test-results table records at least four boundary cases.

title: Support-ticket triage queue
brief: A support lead needs a repeatable way to review tickets. Build a program that reads a small in-memory ticket list, assigns exactly one priority to each valid ticket, and prints a summary. Critical tickets are urgent; other tickets aged at least 24 hours need review; the rest are standard. Invalid or incomplete tickets must be reported instead of silently classified.
deliverables: A triage program with documented rule precedence.
A sample queue containing normal, critical, old, and invalid tickets.
A summary of each priority and rejected records.
A test table for empty queues and threshold cases.
acceptance: Each valid ticket receives exactly one documented priority.
Critical severity takes precedence over the age rule.
The 24-hour boundary behaves as specified.
Invalid records and an empty queue are handled visibly.
Priority totals and rejection totals match the processed records.

title: A reusable quote calculator
brief: A small service business creates quotes with line items and a delivery fee. Build calculation functions using integer cents, plus a thin display layer. Define supported prices and quantities explicitly. The first version has no tax integration, discounts, payments, or live exchange rates; those are separate scope decisions.
deliverables: Calculation functions for line totals, subtotal, and grand total.
A readable example quote with two line items.
A written contract for integer prices and quantities.
Tests for zero, negative, and unsupported inputs.
acceptance: Calculations use documented integer minor units.
Line, subtotal, and grand-total functions return useful values.
The display layer is separate from the calculation functions.
Zero and invalid inputs follow the written contract.
A manually checked quote and regression examples agree with the implementation.

title: Customer contact directory
brief: A small team needs to add, find, update, and list contacts. Build an in-memory directory keyed by stable IDs. Allow duplicate display names, validate required fields, and make a missing ID understandable. Persistence is intentionally left for the next lesson, so today you can concentrate on data shape and operations.
deliverables: A contact model with ID, name, city, and optional email.
Operations to add, look up, update, search, and list records.
A sample dataset containing duplicate names and missing optional values.
An explanation of identity, validation, and ordering decisions.
acceptance: Each contact has a stable unique ID and a non-blank name.
Duplicate display names do not overwrite records.
Lookup and update use IDs and handle missing IDs clearly.
Search does not delete or mutate the original directory.
Required and optional fields are documented and tested.

title: Persistent contact book with recovery
brief: Extend the contact directory so records survive closing and reopening the program. Store them in a documented JSON file, validate loaded records, and distinguish first launch from damaged existing data. Add a recovery message and a backup approach that preserves the user's information while you investigate a failure.
deliverables: Save and load operations with a documented data-file path and format.
A validated contact schema compatible with lesson 5.
A recovery policy for missing, malformed, and invalid files.
A restart test and a debugging log for one controlled failure.
acceptance: Contacts survive a normal process restart.
Loaded data is checked for both JSON syntax and contact shape.
First launch works when the data file is absent.
Corrupt existing data is reported and preserved for recovery.
The README documents the data path, backup, and recovery steps.

title: A usable CLI expense tracker
brief: A freelancer needs to record small expenses and inspect a reliable total. Build a command-line tool that adds, lists, and totals fictional expenses, saves them between runs, and explains invalid input. A stranger should be able to install and use it from the README. Receipt scanning, accounts, and bank connections are outside the first version.
deliverables: An add/list/total command workflow with JSON persistence.
A clear data model and money-unit policy.
A README with setup, sample commands, and error examples.
A recorded user observation and a test-results table.
acceptance: Add, list, and total form a working command-line workflow.
Expenses survive a restart with stable IDs.
Amounts follow a documented numeric representation and validation policy.
A fresh setup works from the README alone.
One usability observation and all test cases are recorded.

title: A reviewed validation feature
brief: A teammate reports that your expense tool accepts an invalid amount. Deliver a targeted fix in a feature branch of your own project repository. Include a reproduction case, tests, updated instructions, and a review description. Preserve unrelated work and make the result easy to inspect before merging.
deliverables: A feature branch containing a bounded behavior change.
Before/after output for the reported input.
A regression test and updated user-facing instructions.
A pull-request-style description and a reviewed diff.
acceptance: The branch is scoped to the reported validation behavior.
A reproduction case documents the original failure.
The regression check fails before the fix and passes after it.
The staged diff contains only the intended code and documentation.
The review description states behavior, tests, and remaining limits.

title: Weather-service adapter with offline fixtures
brief: A travel dashboard needs a city and clearly labelled temperature, but its provider can return incomplete data or fail. Build an adapter with a fixture transport for repeatable tests and an optional live transport based on a provider's current documentation. Keep the UI independent of the provider's payload shape and distinguish offline demonstration data from live results.
deliverables: A documented request/response and internal-result contract.
Fixture cases for valid data, missing data, timeout, and service error.
A validated adapter and a thin display layer.
An explicit retry policy and optional live-provider setup notes.
acceptance: The adapter exposes a documented internal shape with units.
Fixture data is clearly labelled as offline demonstration data.
Malformed, missing, and wrongly typed payloads are rejected clearly.
Timeouts and service errors follow a bounded documented policy.
Transport and parsing can be tested independently.

title: A reproducible release kit
brief: A teammate needs to run your expense tracker on a clean machine or environment. Package the interpreter requirement, dependency installation, configuration examples, data-path policy, and smoke test into a release kit. Keep the original working project intact while you test the clean setup in a separate directory.
deliverables: A setup guide with platform-appropriate commands.
A dependency declaration or an explicit standard-library-only statement.
A non-secret configuration example and data-path explanation.
A smoke test plus evidence from a clean setup.
acceptance: The interpreter requirement and run command are documented.
Dependencies are explicitly declared or identified as standard-library only.
Required configuration is documented with no real secrets.
The data path and working-directory assumptions are clear.
A clean-environment smoke test succeeds using only the written guide.

title: Support-ticket domain model
brief: A help desk needs tickets with stable IDs, readable titles, and controlled status changes. Build a small domain model with create, close, and optional reopen operations. Test invalid creation and repeated transitions. Compare your object-based design with a simpler alternative and explain which one you would use for this scope.
deliverables: A ticket model and a written state-transition policy.
Validation for required identity and title fields.
Tests for normal, invalid, and repeated operations.
A short class-versus-functions design comparison.
acceptance: Tickets have stable IDs and validated non-blank titles.
Supported states and transitions are documented.
Closing an open ticket preserves identity and changes state correctly.
Repeated or invalid transitions follow an explicit policy.
Tests and a simpler-design comparison support the chosen model.

title: A regression suite for the expense calculator
brief: The expense calculator once produced an incorrect total. Build a repeatable test suite that captures that failure, normal calculations, zero values, invalid input, and a storage round trip. Keep the expected results independent and write a short report describing what the suite establishes and what still requires a workflow or provider check.
deliverables: A test module runnable with unittest or pytest.
A regression case for a documented calculation bug.
Boundary, invalid-input, and storage integration cases.
A report of assertions, observed results, and coverage limits.
acceptance: The suite runs with a documented single command.
At least one regression case detects a concrete faulty implementation.
Expected values are independent of the code under test.
Normal, zero, invalid-input, and persistence cases are included.
The test report records results and meaningful verification limits.

title: Responsive expense dashboard
brief: A freelancer wants to add labelled expenses, see a list and total, remove a mistaken record, and return to the data later in the same browser. Build a semantic HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface using fictional data. Document that browser-local persistence is a learning constraint and does not provide shared accounts or server-side authorization.
deliverables: A responsive form, expense list, total, and empty state.
Clear labels, keyboard behavior, and validation messages.
Browser-local persistence with useful handling of damaged saved data.
A usability and narrow-viewport test report.
acceptance: Adding and removing named expenses updates the list and total correctly.
Form controls have visible labels and work with a keyboard.
Invalid input has a useful message and does not change stored data.
Data survives a reload in the same browser with documented limits.
The task works at 375px without page-wide horizontal overflow.

title: A verified public expense dashboard
brief: Publish the dashboard from lesson 13 in your own learner project repository or chosen static host. Verify the deployed site in a clean browser, test a narrow viewport and reload, and record the release identity. Keep setup and recovery instructions alongside the project. Do not change the academy's hosting configuration as part of your learner exercise.
deliverables: A verified public URL and the source commit that produced it.
Build or publishing instructions for the chosen host.
A completed hosted verification checklist.
A release note, known limits, and recovery steps.
acceptance: A public URL serves the intended application version.
Required assets load under the actual hosting path.
Core form and expense workflows pass in a clean browser.
Direct loading, reload, and a narrow viewport are checked.
Release identity and recovery instructions are recorded.

title: LLM experiment and budget notebook
brief: A team is deciding whether a model could help with short support summaries. Create a small experiment record containing prompts, response examples, scoring criteria, latency/usage fields, and a cost estimate. Support an offline fixture mode for learning and an optional real-provider mode. Never combine the two modes into an unlabeled performance claim.
deliverables: An experiment log with model or fixture identity and request settings.
Three prompt cases with a human-readable quality rubric.
A usage/cost calculator with explicit scope and assumptions.
A comparison note distinguishing observations, estimates, and unknowns.
acceptance: Every response is labelled as fixture or observed provider output.
The chosen model/settings or fixture version is recorded.
A quality rubric covers support, completeness, and task fit.
The cost calculation states volume, usage, prices, and included scope.
Results distinguish measurements, estimates, and remaining uncertainty.

title: Versioned support-ticket classifier
brief: A support team wants to route tickets into billing, technical, and general queues. Build a labelled dataset, a versioned prompt, an output validator, and a comparison report. Fixture mode lets you verify the pipeline without provider access; optional real-provider mode lets you collect predictions. Ambiguous and invalid outputs must not silently trigger routing.
deliverables: A label rubric and at least 12 labelled ticket examples.
Versioned prompts with one clearly explained revision.
A parser/validator and an explicit review or rejection result.
A comparison report separating fixture checks from real predictions.
acceptance: Allowed categories and ambiguity policy are documented.
At least 12 labelled examples include boundary and invalid-input cases.
Response parsing validates shape, types, and allowed labels.
Prompt versions and predictions are recorded for comparison.
Fixture checks and real-provider evaluations are reported separately.

title: An allowlisted inventory tool service
brief: A shop assistant needs read-only stock lookup and product search over fictional inventory. Build a dispatcher with two named tools, argument validation, not-found results, and a trusted-user access policy. Demonstrate invalid proposals and resource restrictions with fixtures before optionally connecting a model that proposes tool calls.
deliverables: Two documented read-only tool contracts and a dispatcher.
A fictional inventory dataset and trusted-user policy fixtures.
Tests for invalid names, arguments, and forbidden resources.
A trace of proposal, validation, execution, and tool result.
acceptance: Only the two documented read-only tools can execute.
Names, shapes, types, and ranges are validated before calls.
Trusted user/resource policy is enforced outside model arguments.
Not-found, forbidden, and failed-call results remain distinguishable.
A safe execution trace and invalid-proposal tests are recorded.

title: FAQ retrieval comparison workbench
brief: A team wants staff to find the right FAQ despite variations in wording. Build a small FAQ dataset, a keyword baseline, a vector-search implementation, and labelled query results. Begin with clearly labelled illustrative vectors if needed; optionally add a real embedding model. Compare the methods honestly and preserve a no-match outcome.
deliverables: At least 10 FAQ records with stable IDs and source text.
Keyword and vector ranking functions with clear input contracts.
At least six queries with expected relevant IDs.
A comparison report naming the representation and its limits.
acceptance: FAQ records and query relevance use stable IDs.
Keyword and vector methods are evaluated on the same labelled queries.
Vector dimensions and zero-length inputs are validated.
The vector model or illustrative-fixture identity is recorded.
No-answer queries and observed retrieval failures are reported.

title: Source-grounded FAQ assistant
brief: A team wants answers from a small fictional policy collection. Build a retrieval-and-answer pipeline that preserves source IDs, displays supporting passages, and handles unanswered questions. Use a clearly labelled extractive or fixture baseline first; optionally connect a real model generator without weakening permission or citation checks.
deliverables: A small source collection with IDs, locations, and freshness notes.
A retrieval method with inspectable ranked results.
An answer contract including citations and a no-answer state.
A labelled question set covering support, conflict, and missing evidence.
acceptance: Retrieved evidence retains source IDs and inspectable passages.
Trusted document-access policy is applied before context construction.
Answer citations refer to supplied evidence and support their claims.
Missing evidence produces a clear abstention result.
Retrieval and answer-quality failures are recorded separately.

title: A bounded policy-research assistant
brief: A team needs a short evidence-based summary from approved fictional policy documents. Build a workflow with search, read, and finish actions, then optionally replace scripted action selection with a model adapter. Enforce resource limits, permitted tools, and no-answer behavior in code. The first version is read-only and cannot send messages or modify business records.
deliverables: An allowed-tool contract and fixed or model-selected action interface.
Application-enforced step, timeout, and budget policies.
An inspectable trace of actions and result categories.
Fixtures for success, tool failure, invalid action, and budget exhaustion.
acceptance: Only the documented read-only tools can execute.
Application code enforces step, timeout, and resource policies.
Completion, abstention, failure, and budget exhaustion are distinct.
Observable traces identify actions and results without hidden reasoning.
Success and failure fixtures terminate within the documented limits.

title: A shareable document-assistant demo
brief: Create a usable interface for the grounded assistant from lesson 19. Include example questions, answer/source display, no-evidence and failure states, and an honest mode label. Publish a fictional-data demo or document a reproducible local version while a trusted backend is being prepared. A real-provider extension must keep credentials out of the frontend.
deliverables: A usable interface connected to the validated answer contract.
A fictional/public document collection and scope explanation.
A verified demo URL or a reproducible local delivery record.
A workflow test report and one observed usability improvement.
acceptance: The interface states its document scope and actual execution mode.
Answered results display relevant supporting passages.
No-evidence and service-failure states are distinguishable and useful.
The demo contains no private documents or browser-exposed credentials.
A new-user workflow and delivery verification are recorded.

title: A repeatable document-assistant evaluation harness
brief: Build a harness for at least 20 labelled questions or boundary cases. Run the grounded assistant under a named execution mode, save its actual outputs, score them using a documented rubric, and compare two versions. Include supported answers, no-evidence behavior, permission checks, and failures. Report critical regressions even if an overall average improves.
deliverables: A versioned dataset with at least 20 stable case IDs.
A rubric and repeatable run/scoring command.
Per-case output records and category summaries.
A before/after report identifying regressions and limits.
acceptance: At least 20 labelled cases have stable IDs and documented coverage.
The harness has a repeatable run command and a reviewed rubric.
Actual outputs and execution mode are recorded per case.
Summaries show category counts, denominators, and failed IDs.
A two-version comparison reports regressions and verification limits.

title: A permission and budget boundary for the assistant
brief: Harden the fictional document assistant with trusted-user fixtures, document filtering, request limits, and explicit exhausted-budget behavior. Add a small threat model and abuse test set. Keep the prototype's limits visible: fixture identity and single-process budgets demonstrate boundaries but are not a deployed authentication or distributed-quota system.
deliverables: A trust-boundary diagram and protected-resource list.
Permission filtering before context construction.
Explicit request/resource limits and recovery results.
An abuse-test report and a reproducible cost estimate.
acceptance: Trusted authority is separate from user text and model arguments.
Forbidden documents never enter an unauthorized user's context.
Resource limits are enforced outside the model prompt.
Budget exhaustion and policy rejection produce clear outcomes.
The threat model, attack results, and cost assumptions are recorded.

title: FastAPI feedback and question service
brief: Build POST /feedback, GET /feedback/{id}, and POST /ask for the fictional assistant. Use validated request models, a documented SQLite file, parameterized queries, and a trusted-identity boundary or explicitly labelled local identity fixtures. Reuse your answer contract and make invalid, missing, and forbidden outcomes clear. Verify the current FastAPI installation command in the linked documentation.
deliverables: An API contract and runnable FastAPI service with documented setup.
A durable feedback schema and parameterized storage layer.
Request validation and explicitly scoped access checks.
HTTP, restart, and invalid-input test results.
acceptance: The three endpoints follow documented request/response contracts.
Invalid payloads and domain-rule failures are rejected clearly.
Feedback survives a process restart in the documented database.
Database values use parameterized SQL rather than command concatenation.
Trusted identity or fixture limits and access checks are explicitly tested.

title: Request tracing and an incident runbook
brief: Instrument the fictional assistant's validation, retrieval, answer, and failure stages with structured events and a shared request ID. Create a runbook for a retrieval timeout and a bad release. Measure actual elapsed time where implemented, clearly label fixtures, and avoid unnecessary private content in logs.
deliverables: A structured event schema and correlated request trace.
A redaction/data-minimization policy for logs.
Runbooks for timeout diagnosis and release recovery.
Evidence from a simulated incident and runbook walkthrough.
acceptance: Events from one request share a correlation ID.
Stable event names identify success and failure stages.
Logs omit credentials and unnecessary private content.
Actual measurements and fixture values are clearly distinguished.
Runbooks include symptoms, checks, recovery verification, and ownership.

title: A discovery interview and customer brief
brief: Use the retailer scenario in the app or another clearly fictional business workflow. Conduct a structured roleplay, record evidence and assumptions, compare implementation alternatives, and produce a one-page brief. A real interview is optional and requires authorization from the people involved; the learning project can be completed entirely with fictional data.
deliverables: A discovery-question plan and notes from two roleplays or authorized interviews.
A one-page problem, scope, constraints, and success brief.
A baseline-measurement and evaluation plan.
An alternatives comparison and a risk/owner list.
acceptance: The brief identifies the user and a concrete current workflow.
Measured facts, interview estimates, and unknowns are distinguished.
In-scope and excluded tasks are explicit.
Data access, constraints, and operating ownership are recorded.
Success criteria include a baseline and an evaluation method.

title: An evidence-based portfolio case study
brief: Choose one completed learning project and package it for a reader who has no context. Write a concise case study, verify the repository and demo links, include a representative test report, and explain your own contribution. Use the app's portfolio tracker to keep the artifacts together and export a readable copy.
deliverables: A problem-first case study with scope and contribution.
Verified project links or a clearly documented local demo.
A representative test/evaluation record and actual result.
A small implementation diagram and explicit limits.
acceptance: The case study states a specific user problem and resulting behavior.
Your implementation and decision contribution are clear.
Outcome claims link to evidence or are labelled estimates.
Demo/repository setup or local-delivery instructions are verified.
The architecture, limitations, and next step match the actual project.

title: Customer-policy assistant capstone
brief: Build a fictional customer's read-only policy assistant using a clear interface, trusted backend boundary, source-grounded answer flow, feedback storage, and an evaluation suite. Start with a labelled offline mode if necessary, then add a real provider only when its contract and secret handling are understood. Keep external messaging, purchases, and autonomous writes outside this capstone scope.
deliverables: A scoped customer brief and actual architecture diagram.
A working question-to-evidence-to-answer workflow.
Feedback persistence and clear product failure states.
Acceptance evidence, a repeatable eval suite, and an unfinished-work list.
acceptance: The capstone follows a specific brief with explicit excluded actions.
A complete user question produces supported evidence and a usable response.
Missing evidence and service failure have honest distinct states.
Access policy and feedback persistence are tested at their boundaries.
A repeatable eval report and remaining-work list accompany the implementation.

title: A hardened capstone release package
brief: Take the capstone through a documented release-readiness process. Verify its actual environment, permissions, bounded failures, stored feedback, and operating limits. Rehearse recovery in an isolated setup using fictional data. Produce a release decision with evidence and unresolved checks instead of claiming universal production readiness.
deliverables: A versioned hosted or reproducible release record.
Permission, failure, resource, and data check evidence.
A recovery runbook and isolated rehearsal result.
An operational-owner map and explicit release limitations.
acceptance: The tested release and environment are explicitly identified.
Allowed and forbidden access paths are verified after deployment.
Timeout, provider failure, and budget exhaustion are bounded and visible.
Data durability and recovery compatibility are checked in an isolated rehearsal.
Configuration, alerts, backup, and escalation have documented owners.

title: A customer-ready demo and handoff pack
brief: Package your capstone as a scoped delivery. Record a concise demo, assemble acceptance and evaluation evidence, verify the operating instructions with another person, and write a retrospective. Produce a next-project plan tied to one demonstrated weakness. Do not publish private customer data or send promotional messages as part of this learning exercise.
deliverables: A short demo script or recording tied to actual acceptance criteria.
A versioned delivery pack with operating and recovery instructions.
A handoff walkthrough observation and a corrected documentation gap.
A retrospective and a concrete follow-up learning project.
acceptance: The demo shows a normal workflow and a meaningful failure boundary.
Claims identify the actual release, data scope, and execution mode.
Acceptance and evaluation evidence are linked in the handoff pack.
Another person can follow operating instructions with documented roles and recovery.
A retrospective and evidence-based next project are recorded.
